I trained it with the `chemprop` command-line tool (version 2.3.1) for 20 epochs on `data/solubility.csv`:

```
chemprop train -i data/solubility.csv -s smiles --target-columns logS \
  --task-type regression --epochs 20 -o out --metrics rmse
```

- **Split:** I used chemprop's default random 80/10/10 split, so the test set is 50 of the 500 molecules.
- **Check:** I recalculated the RMSE myself from `out/model_0/test_predictions.csv` and the test rows listed in `out/splits.json`, and got the same number.
- **Model:** The checkpoint that scored best on validation was from the last epoch (epoch 19). The model is saved at `out/model_0/best.pt`.

This is a quick 20-epoch run, so the model probably isn't fully trained, and with only 50 test molecules the RMSE will vary between random splits.

I trained a Chemprop 2.3.1 model on `data/solubility.csv` for 20 epochs and saved its `logS` predictions for all 10 molecules in `data/new_molecules.csv` to `predictions.csv`. The model is accurate only to about ±1.2 log units, so treat these as rough estimates.

- **Training:** I used the default settings, a random 400/50/50 split (training, validation and test), and ran on the CPU. The best checkpoint came from the last epoch (19, validation loss 0.35), which suggests the model was still improving when training stopped at the 20-epoch limit.

- **Data and split:** `data/solubility.csv` has 500 molecules. I used the default random 80/10/10 train/validation/test split.
- **Training:** a regression model on `logS`, run for 20 epochs on CPU. Chemprop keeps the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss and scores that one on the test set.
- **Output:** the model is saved at `runs/logS/model_0/best.pt`.

Two things to keep in mind when reading the number:
- **It will vary between runs.** I didn't fix a seed, so retraining will give a somewhat different RMSE. Adding `--pytorch-seed` would make it repeatable.
- **It's likely optimistic.** A random split usually overstates how well the model does on molecules unlike its training data.

I trained it with `chemprop train -i data/solubility.csv -s smiles --target-columns logS -t regression --epochs 20 -o out`, which uses the default random 80/10/10 train/validation/test split. The best checkpoint came from the last epoch (epoch 19), with a validation loss of 0.40. Validation loss was still dropping at that point, so the 20-epoch cap probably stopped it before it fully converged.

Chemprop's default test metric is MSE rather than RMSE, and it reported 1.4193. To get the RMSE, I compared the saved test predictions (`out/model_0/test_predictions.csv`) with the true `logS` values for the test rows listed in `out/splits.json`. That gave 1.19135, which matches the square root of the reported MSE.

I trained two models for 20 epochs each, on CPU, using Chemprop's default random 80/10/10 train/validation/test split:

| Model | Test RMSE | Test MAE | Test R² |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trained from scratch | 1.17 | 0.91 | 0.40 |
| **Fine-tuned from CheMeleon** (used for predictions) | **0.73** | **0.49** | **0.77** |

CheMeleon is a pretrained model that Chemprop can fine-tune, which helps on small datasets like this one. Its weights were already saved on this machine, so no download was needed. A random split tends to make test scores look better than they will be on molecules unlike the training set.

**Check against measured values:** `data/measured_solubility.csv` has measured `logS` for all 10 new molecules. None of them are in the training data. The predictions are off by 0.29 log units on average, though 10 molecules is too few to mean much.

The model is saved at `runs/logS_chemeleon/model_0/best.pt`; the from-scratch model is in `runs/logS`.
